title: The date of Easter
hookLine: Nicaea also sought one date for Easter, still not shared by all Christians

lines: A SPRING FEAST, RECKONED BY THE MOON.
cards: "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." That's Saint Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. The pasch is the Passover; Paul calls Christ the Passover lamb.
So the feast of the resurrection grew up in the Passover season, a spring feast reckoned by the moon. And reckoning by the moon is harder than it sounds. Which full moon?
Which Sunday after it? The historian Eusebius records that, well before Nicaea, churches in different places had answered those questions differently.
Today, the other question the bishops carried to Nicaea: the date of Easter.

teach.b: Who the Son is was the great question at Nicaea. But by the account Eusebius preserves, the council also took up something that sounds smaller: the day of Easter.

Eusebius keeps a letter the emperor Constantine sent to the churches after the council, urging everyone to keep the feast on one and the same day, so the Church would not be split over the feast of the resurrection.
A practical problem with a deep root: if one church is still fasting while the church down the road is singing alleluia, does it look like one Church? The hope at Nicaea was a single day.
Over the centuries, though, East and West came to reckon the date by different calendars.
Today Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep the same resurrection, in some years on the same Sunday, and in some years not.
Notice what this disagreement is not.
It isn't about whether Christ rose; both proclaim it. It's a quarrel about the calendar, which is part of why it aches: so small, and still unsettled.
The Second Vatican Council said it would not object to fixing Easter on a set Sunday, provided the other churches agreed.

teach.h: VATICAN II LEFT THE DOOR OPEN.
teach.b: The door is open; nobody has walked through it alone, because the whole point is to walk through together. One day, someday.
This week ran from Kyiv's river and the two lungs, through the Fathers, to the councils: what a council is, Nicaea, one word for who the Son is, and today, one day for the feast.

how: Catholics and Orthodox Christians in the same town sometimes keep Easter on different Sundays, and some families of mixed churches keep both; the Catholic Church has said it is open to a common date if the other churches agree.

games.q: you're at Nicaea. churches in different places keep Easter on different days. what do you hope for?
o: let every church keep its own day forever.
one and the same day for the whole Church.

games.why: by Eusebius's account, the emperor's letter after the council urges one and the same day for all.

practice: Bring to mind someone who keeps Easter on a different Sunday, an Orthodox neighbor, a coworker, a family across the world, or any two people you love who can't land on a date for anything, and hold both in one breath without trying to solve it.
If you pray, ask God for the day when the whole Church sings alleluia on the same morning; if you don't, just wish it for them.

wordCard.voice: Pasch, the Passover, the word Paul uses for Christ, and the season when Nicaea hoped every church would keep the resurrection on one day. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the Passover, and in Christian Greek the feast of Easter; Paul calls Christ our pasch.

carryVoice: Your line: one day, someday. The same resurrection, still waiting on the same Sunday. Day seven hundred seventy, done.
